questions.prompt: A city surveys 400 randomly chosen residents, and 62% of them support a new park. Which identifies the population, sample, parameter, and statistic correctly?
questions.prompt_markup: A city surveys 400 randomly chosen residents, and 62% of them support a new park. Which identifies the population, sample, parameter, and statistic correctly?

choices.text: Population: all residents; sample: the 62% who support it; parameter: 400; statistic: 62%.
Population: all residents; sample: the 400 surveyed; parameter: percent of all residents in support; statistic: 62%.
Population: the 400 surveyed; sample: all residents; parameter: 62%; statistic: percent of all residents in support.
Population: all residents; sample: the 400 surveyed; parameter: 62%; statistic: percent of all residents in support.

questions.correct_answer: Population: all residents; sample: the 400 surveyed; parameter: percent of all residents in support; statistic: 62%.
questions.grading_note: A parameter describes the population; a statistic describes the sample.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Distinguish population, sample, parameter, and statistic
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why does a random sample allow conclusions about the whole population?
questions.prompt_markup: Why does a random sample allow conclusions about the whole population?

choices.text: A random sample always includes every member of the population, so nothing is left out of it.
Chance decides who is chosen, so the sample tends to represent the population without systematic bias.
A random sample is always larger than a voluntary sample, so its result is always more exact.
A random sample always has exactly the same statistic as the population parameter it estimates.

questions.correct_answer: Chance decides who is chosen, so the sample tends to represent the population without systematic bias.
questions.grading_note: Random selection removes selection bias; chance variation remains. The others are false: a sample does not include everyone, is not always larger, and does not match the parameter exactly.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability
questions.prompt: Why do studies often use a sample instead of the whole population?
questions.prompt_markup: Why do studies often use a sample instead of the whole population?

choices.text: Samples have no chance variation at all.
Samples always give the exact population value.
A population cannot be described by a number.

questions.correct_answer: Studying everyone may be too costly, slow, or impossible.
questions.grading_note: Practical limits. The others are false: samples do vary by chance, do not give the exact population value, and populations are described by numbers.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability
questions.prompt: Why is a larger random sample usually better for estimating a population value?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is a larger random sample usually better for estimating a population value?

choices.text: Its statistic varies less from sample to sample, so the estimate is more precise.
It always gives exactly the population value, with no chance variation.
It makes the population value larger, so the estimate is closer to it.
It removes all bias, even when the sample is not chosen at random.

questions.correct_answer: Its statistic varies less from sample to sample, so the estimate is more precise.
questions.grading_note: Less sampling variability. The others are false: no sample gives the exact value, size does not change the population, and size does not remove bias.
